phonemes.desc: Short o as in 'more'; Hawaiian syllables are always open.
Light li; the name is usually parsed poli 'bosom' + ahu 'garment, cloak.'
The stressed syllable — Hawaiian stress falls on the penult here.
Final hu with a soft, breathy h.

pronunciation.approximation: 'poh-lee-AH-hoo' — stress on the third syllable; every vowel is sounded separately.

kin.label: Hawaiian name
kin.form: Poliahu, from poli 'bosom, embrace' + ahu 'garment, cloak' — 'cloaked bosom' (Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary)

kin.label: Her sisters
kin.form: Lilinoe (mist of Mauna Kea), Waiau (of Lake Waiau), and Kahoupokane — the snow-maiden kin of the mountain

kin.label: Her rival
kin.form: Pele, the volcano goddess of Kīlauea — the fire against her snow

pronunciation.note: Poliahu is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration carries no macron or ʻokina, so ASCII loses nothing the canonical form preserves. The lexicon gloss 'Cloaked bosom' follows the standard dictionary parsing (poli + ahu) given in Pukui & Elbert.

domains.title: Poliahu
domains.subtitle: Snow
domains.lead: Poliahu is the Hawaiian goddess of snow — the beautiful and powerful mistress of Mauna Kea's summit, whose white mantle crowns the highest mountain in the Pacific and whose duel with the volcano goddess Pele for possession of the mountain is one of Hawai'i's most beloved and most retold legends.

cards.name: Mistress of Mauna Kea
cards.desc: She dwells on the summit of the White Mountain, wrapping its peak in snow and mist.

cards.name: The Snow Mantle
cards.desc: Her cloak of snow — beauty that can fall as hail and blizzard when she is angered.

cards.name: Rival of Pele
cards.desc: She met Pele in the legendary hōlua sled race and drove the fire goddess back with snow and hail.

cards.name: Guardian of the Heights
cards.desc: Lake Waiau and the summit region are her household — the sacred cold at the island's crown.

symbols.name: The Snow Mantle (Kahiko)
symbols.meaning: Her garment of snow spread over Mauna Kea — the 'cloaked bosom' of her name

symbols.name: The Hōlua Sled
symbols.meaning: Her racing sled from the great contest with Pele — beauty in swift, sure motion

symbols.name: Lake Waiau
symbols.meaning: The sacred summit lake, home of her sister Waiau — one of Hawai'i's most revered waters

symbols.name: The Summit Shrines (Ahu)
symbols.meaning: The stone shrines of Mauna Kea's peak, built within her sight over a thousand years

symbols.name: Hail and Mist
symbols.meaning: Her two tempers — the soft mist of welcome and the stinging hail of her anger

mythology.lead: Poliahu's mythology is preserved chiefly in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Hawaiian-language and Hawaiian-authored texts — above all Emma Nakuina's Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends (1904), synthesized in Beckwith's Hawaiian Mythology (1970). Its centerpiece is the great contest of snow and fire for the mountain, a duel that Hawaiians read in the island's very lava flows and snowfields to this day.

myths.title: The Stranger on the Mountain
myths.text: On the slopes of Mauna Kea, Poliahu and her snow-sister friends were challenged to a hōlua sled race by a beautiful stranger. The stranger lost — and flung off her disguise: she was Pele, goddess of volcanoes, and she erupted in fire down the mountainside (Nakuina, Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends, 1904; retold in Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology, 1970, and Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, 1916). Poliahu rose to her full height and answered with snow and hail, beating the flames back. The race ran on the great hōlua slide of the mountain's flank, whose stone track can still be traced — the legend pins its scene to a course its first audience knew. The battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountainThe battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountain — fire trenches, snowfields — and the legend still reads the landscape: every cinder and snowbank on Mauna Kea is a stroke of that duel.

myths.title: The Household of the Peak
myths.text: Poliahu does not keep the summit alone. Her companions are her sisters — Lilinoe, who rules the mountain's mists, Waiau, who dwells in the sacred lake that bears her name, and Kahoupokane — together the cold maidens of the high mountain (Nakuina 1904; Beckwith 1970). Waiau's water lies nearly four thousand meters above the sea and never truly warms; tradition held it cold and pure as the goddess herself, and chiefs drank of it only after ceremony. Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania,Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania, was kapu — its water reserved for the highest chiefs and for the goddess's own uses. The mythology does the work of a natural history: it distributes the summit's phenomena — snow, mist, lake, wind — among a family, making the mountain a household rather than a heap of rock.

myths.title: Poliahu and ʻAiwohikupua
myths.text: The Kauaʻi chief ʻAiwohikupua came to the mountain and won the goddess's love — but he was betrothed to a woman of his own island, and Poliahu discovered the truth. Her anger fell on him like weather: he shivered at her touch, and when he fled homeward she sent the cold after him — snow fell on Kauaʻi's heights, a sign of her reach (the legend cycle as recorded in Beckwith 1970, from the Hawaiian-language newspapers; Westervelt 1916 gives a parallel). The courtship also explains the weather: the snow that touches Kaua'i's peaks on the rarest nights is Poliahu's answer still, and old Kaua'i families retold it as a standing warning to oath-breaking chiefs. The tale carries a chiefly moral in goddess form:The tale carries a chiefly moral in goddess form: love given to a sworn heart is a debt the weather itself will collect.

myths.title: The Great Battle for the Mountain
myths.text: The full combat of Poliahu and Pele — the longest form of the legend — raged from Mauna Kea down toward the sea: Pele vomiting rivers of lava, Poliahu calling up snowstorms and hail, the land between them torn and remade, until the fire was driven to its own country in the south and the white mountain stood (Nakuina 1904; Beckwith 1970). Modern kūpuna retell the battle as an account of balance — that the island needs both fire and snow, and that it is the goddesses' long truce, not either one's victory, which keeps the land alive. Hawaiians watching real eruptions reach toward Mauna Kea's snowsHawaiians watching real eruptions reach toward Mauna Kea's snows had the myth for what they saw. Read geologically, the story is a memory of the islands' living duel of elements; read theologically, it grants the cold goddess and the hot one equal sovereignty — fire rules the rift, snow rules the summit, and the island is their treaty line.

lore.syncretism: Christianization in Hawaiʻi suppressed the goddess cults, but Poliahu survived in a characteristic Hawaiian mode: through the Hawaiian-language newspapers of the nineteenth century and through authors such as Emma Nakuina — a Hawaiian woman writing in English in 1904 — who preserved the legends while Victorian ethnographers were flattening them. In the twentieth century, a modern form of identification emerged: Poliahu became the patroness of Mauna Kea's defense. During the protests against telescope construction on the summit — most visibly the 2014–2019 movement against the Thirty Meter Telescope — kiaʻi (guardians) invoked her name and her snow: the mountain, they argued, is her body and her home, and science must kneel at the summit as at a temple. The goddess of the snow mantle thus became a contemporary standard-bearer for Hawaiian sovereignty over sacred land.
lore.culturalLegacy: Poliahu's cult center was the summit itself: Lake Waiau, still sacred, and the dozens of stone shrines that crown the mountain. Offerings of lei and hoʻokupu continue at the lake in the present day, and her name is taught in Hawaiian-medium schools as part of the island's own natural history. In the broader culture she is the personification of Mauna Kea's snow — the sight of the white peak above tropical Hilo remains, for many Hawaiians, her visible presence. Her legend cycle anchors a children's and school literature in Hawaiian, and her duel with Pele is the standard telling through which Hawaiians explain the island's two volcanoes-in-character. Since the telescope protests, her name has appeared on signs, chants, and banners across the world — a snow goddess become an emblem of a people's claim to their own mountain.
lore.extendedMeditation: Poliahu embodies a wonder unique in the Pacific: snow in the tropics. Hawaiians, meeting white on a tropical summit, made it a goddess — and the making says something precise about Polynesian theology, which found the sacred in the anomalous and the extreme. Where Pele is appetite and eruption, Poliahu is reserve and stillness; the two goddesses are the island's two temperatures, and the myth grants each her jurisdiction. There is also a geography lesson folded into the myth: the legend's battle-scarred terrain matches real volcanic features reaching toward the snows, so the story functions as memory of eruptions older than any chant. But beyond scholarship, Poliahu endures because she is beautiful in the strict sense — a presence that caps the island with white, that can bless a sled race or bury a valley in hail. She is what a mountain means when the mountain is loved.
lore.archaeology: Mauna Kea's summit preserves one of the most remarkable ritual landscapes in Polynesia. Archaeological surveys (notably Patrick McCoy's work from the 1970s–80s) documented well over a hundred stone shrines (ahu) above 13,000 feet, platforms, burials, and marker cairns clustering around the summit and Lake Waiau — a sacred precinct used for roughly a millennium before Western contact. The mountain's slopes hold the great Keanakākoʻi adze quarry, where Hawaiians knapped summit basalt into tools across many centuries, its workshops marked by vast scatters of flakes and preforms. Lake Waiau itself was a kapu water source, its sediments holding a continuous record of human presence. No image of Poliahu is known — the shrines are her portrait: a mountain-top kept like a heiau, its snow the goddess's own visible temple.
